# Welcome {.unnumbered}

**Hear why a bass line works—and design one deliberately.**

After reading *Thinking in Groove*, you will hear low notes as choices about foundation, direction, time, and interaction, not as a collection of roots beneath chord symbols.

> **Role → Motion → Groove → Interaction → Variation**

The piano is this book's analytical laboratory, not its technical goal. The left hand represents a realistic, monophonic bass line. The right hand supplies the harmony, pulse, space, and conversation that give the bass meaning. Chord symbols show the map; annotations identify only the decision under study.

The format works for bassists, pianists, composers, arrangers, producers, and any musician who wants a practical model of bass-line construction. A bass player can practise the lower staff alone; two musicians can divide the staves; a producer can treat them as separate MIDI roles.

## Start with one audible decision

[Chapter 3, **The Inverter**](chapters/part-1-role/03-the-inverter.md) is the piano-edition prototype. Its A/B laboratory keeps the right hand fixed while one bass note changes the balance of the entire chord. Use **Full**, **Bass only**, and **Harmony only** playback to prove what changed.

## Choose a path

- **New to bass-line design:** begin with Part I and ask what responsibility the bass has.
- **Studying harmony:** hear how inversions and routes reorganize chords.
- **Studying groove:** separate written attack, duration, and space from performed microtiming.
- **Composing or arranging:** follow the complete design sequence from Role through Variation.

Notation can represent pitch, written rhythm, duration, accent, articulation, and register. It cannot fully encode touch, microtiming, ensemble response, or a stable performed pocket. Playback is therefore a listening reference, not a claim that notation captures a human performance.
